Summarize Brown Heart Assistant..answer: Pranav built the Brown Heart Assistant (BHAI) from the ground up as a full‑stack, citation‑grounded health‑education platform that now serves over 5,000 users and also powers a searchable FAQ site [1]. The system uses a router‑orchestrated multi‑agent architecture that routes queries to specialized agents (FAQ, MASALA Study, Instagram, YouTube, movie‑timestamp) and applies confidence gating, source‑grounded prompts, and medical‑safety refusal filters to ensure safe answers [1]. Its retrieval layer combines BM25, Azure PostgreSQL/pgvector, HNSWlib, and NVIDIA embeddings with reciprocal‑rank‑fusion, while Azure OpenAI handles chat generation; a human‑in‑the‑loop (HITL) interface escalates low‑confidence medical queries for doctor‑specialty matching or appointment booking [2]. Production hardening includes Azure Blob artifact hydration, checksum validation, signed sessions, admin health checks, environment‑based model configuration, LangSmith tracing across agent runs and retrieval scores, and a suite of 113 passing tests [2]. In his case‑study, Pranav explains why a “refuse‑and‑route” design is essential for medical Q&A and details the HITL escalation and extensive testing that underpin the system’s reliability [3].

How does he approach RAG reliability?.answer: Pranav tackles RAG reliability by designing self‑correcting architectures that continuously audit and refine their own outputs. He combines query analysis with hybrid retrieval—mixing dense vector search (FAISS/Pinecone) and BM25—while grounding results in a Neo4j knowledge graph, then runs multi‑step evidence‑sufficiency audits and applies confidence‑gating thresholds and safety‑refusal filters to block hallucinations[1]. In his Agentic Graph‑RAG (The Brain) system, a LangGraph agent expands failed queries using HyDE, pulls additional context from the web via Tavily, verifies supporting snippets, and refines queries before answering, which lifted hit rates from 82 % to 92 % and faithfulness scores from 0.708 to 0.847[2]. This layered approach—hybrid retrieval, graph grounding, evidence auditing, and automated query refinement—forms the core of his RAG reliability strategy[3].

citations.snippet: Pranav approaches RAG reliability by building self-correcting architectures. In projects like Agentic Graph-RAG (The Brain) and Brown Heart Assistant, he ensures high reliability using query analysis, hybrid retrieval (BM25 + vector matching), Neo4j knowledge graphs, multi-step evidence sufficiency audits, confidence gating thresholds, and medical-safety refusal filters to prevent hallucinations.

citations.title: Agentic Graph-RAG: The Brain
citations.snippet: Pranav built 'Agentic Graph-RAG: The Brain', a self-correcting LangGraph agent that audits evidence sufficiency, expands searches to web/Wikipedia via Tavily when needed, verifies supporting snippets, and refines failed queries with HyDE query expansion before answering. It uses hybrid retrieval across FAISS/Pinecone dense vectors, BM25, and a 311K-node / 374K-edge Neo4j knowledge graph over 39K chunks, unified with NVIDIA and Cross-Encoder reranking. On 100 judged SQuAD-style examples it improved retrieval hit rate from 82% to 92% and LLM-judged faithfulness from 0.708 to 0.847.

citations.title: Case Study: Agentic Graph-RAG (The Brain)
citations.snippet: Pranav wrote a full case study on Agentic Graph-RAG: The Brain, covering the problem with naive RAG (generating fluent but unsupported answers when retrieval fails), the hybrid FAISS/Pinecone/BM25/Neo4j architecture, the self-correction loop with sufficiency auditing and bounded query refinement, and the results (82%→92% hit rate, 0.708→0.847 faithfulness).
